title: A' Ghaoth Dhubh strips the east coast
summary: A storm out of the south-east strikes before dawn with almost no warning, stripping the thatch from every roof between Cuan ruadh and Ceann chiar and driving three unhauled boats onto the rocks below the headland. No one of that coast dies in it, though many households lose stores, shelter and boats within a single day.

title: The coast's fishing fails before winter begins
summary: Of Cuan ruadh's eleven boats, four are broken past mending and a fifth needs a new keel; granaries stand open to the sky along the whole stripped coast. A fishing that has never in memory failed outright fails that winter for want of boats and stores enough to work it.

title: The coast names the storm A' Ghaoth Dhubh
summary: The eldest of that coast, having no name ready when the storm struck, name it afterward for the ash-dark sky it leaves behind for three days. No reciter of the hill amends the name; every storm to strike that shore since is measured against it.

title: Inland valleys hear of the coast's ruin
summary: A trader who meant to buy salt fish at Cuan ruadh finds instead a shore of broken boats and bare roof-trees, and carries word of it a day and more west to valleys that had never before troubled themselves over that coast's weather.

title: The valleys send grain to Cuan ruadh unasked
summary: Single households send what they can spare because a neighbour has already sent something, until the scatter of gifts grows too large for any one house to account for, and the valleys' holders agree to weigh and send it on by the count of mouths, as the sharing is kept at Dùn ìseal, though none there had been taught the custom directly.

title: The sharing reaches the east coast
summary: Grain, salted meat and wool for roofing come down to Cuan ruadh through the winter on carts and cattle-backs, weighed by mouths and given without reckoning who at the coast has lost most. No household of that coast starves; the coast calls the custom only the bringing-in, or the help.

title: Lìleas begins to watch the dark return of the boats
summary: One-and-twenty that hard winter, with her father's hand maimed and the household's boat unfit to swim, Lìleas of Cuan ruadh spends idle hours on the shingle and comes to notice what the coast has never put into words: that a boat coming home after dark has nothing to steer the last stretch by but memory and the sound of the surf.

title: Lìleas's household agrees to the fire
summary: Lìleas puts the keeping of a fire on the cape east of the village to her own household over a thin meal; her father, no longer trusting his maimed hand on a line, sees no harm in it and asks only that she carry the work herself.

title: The eastern fire is first kept
summary: Lìleas and her younger brother carry driftwood and peat up the cape through a month of short winter days and build the fire in a stone-walled pit, driving flame and smoke seaward. She keeps it alone through nights that find no boat needing it, and more than one household of the village climbs the cape only to sit an hour with her.

title: Word of the eastern fire travels the coast roads
summary: Traders and travellers carry word of the fire on Cuan ruadh's cape along the roads faster than its own light could reach, and coasts that have suffered their own bad weather begin to want fires of their own.

title: A fire is raised on the northern point
summary: On ground already scorched black by older shore-fires, the households of the hardest-running coast raise a fire that burns steadier from its first season, having Lìleas's year of trial to learn by before laying their own wood.

title: Seathan mac Pheadair keeps the north-eastern fire
summary: On the cape where the passage to the deeper water runs narrowest, a man named Seathan mac Pheadair takes up the keeping of a fire much as Lìleas had, and cuts a stroke on a stone at its edge for every ship's light he sees pass safe by it.

title: The southern cape completes the five fires
summary: Last of the four new fires and by every account the surest, the households of the southern cape raise theirs on a mound of stacked stone breast-high, clear of the spray. With the older fire on the Baile chrom headland, the coasts of Dia-thìr are now lit at five points.

title: A reciter names them the five fires
summary: Before the southern mound is even finished, a reciter of that coast says that a boat lost off any shore of Dia-thìr now has a fire somewhere within its sight to steer toward, and names the five together the five fires, a name the coast keeps on every telling since.

title: A boat is brought home to the eastern fire
summary: Blown off its own water by a wind that will not hold steady, a boat out of a coast two villages north finds the coast of Dia-thìr only by Lìleas's fire, burning high on the cape with no house near it. The crew comes ashore whole, and Lìleas tells the captain the fire is kept for whichever boat needs it, no more for him than for any other.
